title: IP Authentication Header
summary: Describes an updated version of the IP Authentication Header, which provides authentication services in IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces RFC 2402 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A tamper-proof seal on each packet that proves who sent it and that nobody changed it on the way.

questions: what is the ipsec authentication header
ah transport mode vs tunnel mode
subtitle: A tamper-evident seal for IP packets: proves who sent them, that nobody altered them, and that they are not replays.

tldr.problem: IP packets can be forged, altered in transit or captured and sent again, and plain IP gives a receiver no way to tell.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication Header (AH) adds a header with a Security Parameters Index, a sequence number and an Integrity Check Value computed over the packet, so the receiver can verify the sender and detect changes and replays.
tldr.outcome: AH gives integrity but no encryption, and it can only protect IP header fields that do not change in transit. This version obsoletes RFC 2402 and adds 64-bit extended sequence numbers.

today: RFC 4302 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005 that obsoletes RFC 2402. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What AH Provides
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header (AH) provides connectionless integrity and data origin authentication for IP datagrams (the RFC calls both just "integrity") and protection against replays. The anti-replay service is optional and is selected by the receiver when a Security Association (SA) is established. The sender always increments the sequence number, but the service only works if the receiver checks it.

AH protects as much of the IP header as possible, plus the next-level protocol data. Some header fields change in transit in ways the sender cannot predict, so AH cannot protect them. The RFC describes the protection of the IP header as "piecemeal".

AH can be used alone, together with the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) or nested. ESP can give the same anti-replay and similar integrity services and also offers encryption. The main difference in integrity is coverage: ESP does not protect IP header fields unless they are encapsulated by ESP, for example in tunnel mode.
sections.plainLanguage: AH is a wax seal on a letter. It does not hide what is written inside, but it shows if someone opened it, and it shows who sealed it.

sections.title: The Authentication Header Format
sections.content:
The header that comes right before AH (an IPv4, IPv6 or extension header) carries the value 51 in its Protocol or Next Header field. AH itself has six parts, and all are mandatory: Next Header (8 bits), Payload Len (8 bits), a Reserved field (16 bits), the Security Parameters Index (SPI, 32 bits), the Sequence Number (32 bits) and a variable-length Integrity Check Value (ICV).

Next Header names the protocol that follows, for example 4 for IPv4, 41 for IPv6 and 6 for TCP. Payload Len is the length of AH in 32-bit words minus 2. With a 96-bit ICV it is 4. Reserved MUST be set to zero by the sender and SHOULD be ignored by the recipient, though it is included in the ICV calculation.

The SPI is an arbitrary 32-bit value the receiver uses to find the SA a packet belongs to. Values 1 through 255 are reserved by IANA. The value zero is for local use and MUST NOT be sent on the wire. The ICV must be a multiple of 32 bits, with explicit padding if needed so that AH is a multiple of 32 bits (IPv4) or 64 bits (IPv6). AH has no version number, so peers must agree on versions through a signalling mechanism such as IKE or out-of-band configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a small label stuck on each packet. It says what is inside, which secret agreement to use, which number in the series this packet is, and holds the seal itself.

sections.title: Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode
sections.content:
In transport mode, AH is inserted after the IP header (and any IPv4 options) and before the next-layer protocol such as TCP, UDP or ICMP, or before any IPsec headers already inserted. In IPv6, AH is treated as an end-to-end payload and so appears after the hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers. The destination options header can appear before or after AH, or both.

In tunnel mode, an inner IP header carries the final source and destination addresses and an outer IP header carries the addresses of the IPsec peers, such as security gateways. Mixed versions are allowed, IPv6 over IPv4 and IPv4 over IPv6. AH protects the whole inner packet, including the inner IP header, and sits in the same position relative to the outer header as in transport mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport mode puts the seal on the letter itself. Tunnel mode puts the whole letter inside a new envelope and seals that, so even the original address is protected.

sections.title: How the Integrity Check Value Is Computed
sections.content:
The ICV covers the IP and extension header fields before AH that are either immutable in transit or predictable on arrival, the AH header itself (with the ICV field set to zero), everything after AH, and the high-order bits of the sequence number when extended sequence numbers are used. The algorithm is set by the SA. Suitable choices include keyed message authentication codes built on a cipher such as AES or on a hash such as MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-256.

Fields that may change in transit are set to zero for the calculation. Zero is used instead of leaving the field out, which preserves alignment and ensures that the field's length cannot be changed in transit. Fields that change but are predictable at the receiver, such as the destination address when source routing is used, are filled in with the value the receiver will see.

For IPv4, the mutable fields are the DSCP, ECN, Flags, Fragment Offset, TTL and Header Checksum. For IPv6 they are DSCP, ECN, Flow Label and Hop Limit. The Flow Label is left out of the ICV to stay compatible with existing AH implementations. IPv4 options have no mutability tag, so Appendix A lists them. If an option is classified as mutable, the whole option is zeroed.

Some algorithms need input in blocks. In that case implicit padding of zero bytes is appended before the calculation. It is not transmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: To make the seal, the sender mixes the packet with a secret key. Parts that routers legitimately change on the way, like a hop counter, are blanked out first so they do not break the seal.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Anti-Replay
sections.content:
On the way out, the sender sets its counter to 0 when the SA is created. It increments the counter for each packet, so the first packet carries sequence number 1. If anti-replay is enabled (the default), the sender MUST NOT send a packet that would make the counter cycle, so a new SA must be set up before the 2^32nd packet. If the counter would overflow, that is an auditable event. With extended sequence numbers (ESN) the counter is 64 bits wide, but only the low-order 32 bits are transmitted. The high-order 32 bits are tracked by both ends and included in the ICV.

On the way in, IP fragments are not accepted: if the offset is nonzero or the More Fragments flag is set, the receiver MUST discard the packet. Reassembly happens before AH processing. The receiver finds the SA in its Security Association Database. For multicast it searches first on SPI, destination and source address, then on SPI and destination address, then on SPI alone or SPI plus protocol. If there is no SA, the packet MUST be discarded.

If anti-replay is on, the receiver checks the sequence number first, using a sliding window. A minimum window of 32 packets MUST be supported, and 64 is preferred as the default. The window is updated only after the ICV is verified. If the ICV check fails, the packet MUST be discarded.

With ESN, the receiver works out the missing high-order bits from its own counter and window (Appendix B). If there is a gap of 2^32 or more consecutive lost packets, the receiver can lose sync. The RFC describes a recovery method where, after a local threshold of consecutive failures, a bad packet is retried with successively larger high-order values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet gets a number, like tickets at a deli counter. The receiver keeps a list of recent tickets and throws away any it has already seen, so a copied packet is spotted.

sections.title: Auditing and Conformance
sections.content:
If AH is built into a system that supports auditing, the AH implementation MUST support auditing and let an administrator turn it on or off. The RFC names auditable events, such as discarding a packet for no SA, a failed ICV or a sequence number overflow, and says what an audit log entry SHOULD contain, typically the SPI, date and time, and source and destination addresses. A receiver is not required to send any message to the apparent sender when it detects such an event, because that could be used for denial of service.

A conforming implementation MUST fully implement AH for unicast traffic and MUST comply with the Security Architecture document, RFC 4301. If it supports multicast it MUST also meet the multicast requirements. Anti-replay SHOULD NOT be offered on manually keyed SAs, because there is no automated recovery if the counter is about to overflow. The mandatory-to-implement algorithms live in a separate RFC, RFC 4305.
sections.plainLanguage: If the system keeps a diary, it must write down when it throws away a suspicious packet. It does not shout back at the sender, since that could be a trick to make it do extra work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's own security section is short: security is central to the design of the protocol, so the considerations run through the whole specification. Further security-relevant aspects of using IPsec are left to the Security Architecture document.

Several points that matter come from elsewhere in the text. Fragments are a denial-of-service risk because a receiver must accept them for reassembly, so an AH implementation MAY choose not to support fragmentation and MUST support generation of ICMP PMTU messages. The Router Alert option is called potentially incompatible with IPsec, and adding or removing security labels on the path conflicts with treating those options as immutable.
sections.plainLanguage: The design is all about security, so there is no separate list of worries. The main warning is that tricks with broken-up packets can make a receiver do extra work.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 2402
sections.content:
This document replaces RFC 2402 and changes three things. First, the SPI rules now give one lookup algorithm for unicast and multicast SAs, covering a wider range of multicast technologies. For unicast the SPI may be used alone or combined with the protocol, at the receiver's option. For multicast the SPI is combined with the destination address and optionally the source address.

Second, a new option for a 64-bit extended sequence number was added for very high-speed communication, along with clarified rules for multicast and multi-sender SAs. Third, the references to mandatory algorithms were moved into a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: The update made it work for group messages, added a bigger ticket counter for very fast networks, and moved the list of approved secret-code recipes to its own book.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the payload that follows AH.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero when sent; covered by the ICV.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Per-SA counter; low-order 32 bits when ESN is used.

fields.name: Integrity Check Value (variable)
fields.desc: Variable length, an integral multiple of 32 bits.
